source.version_note: 2024 journal issue; article copyright is 2023. The repository cover is included in the 14 PDF pages.

reading.source_scope_note: A narrative interdisciplinary synthesis, explicitly not a systematic review or a new participant experiment. Its cited primary experiments, including Logg et al. 2019, were not independently read in this step; the separately reviewed Rastogi preprint remains its own record.
access_limits: All 14 extracted PDF pages read, including the repository cover, sole substantive table, discussion, limitations and references. No result plot required independent digitization.
The review’s cited datasets, protocols and models were not independently reanalyzed; no pooled participant total or new meta-analysis is claimed.

study.design: Narrative theoretical/empirical synthesis of performance-related AI-assisted decisions
study.focus: Human–AI complementarity, people’s mental models of AI, and interaction design
study.scope: Independent decision tasks and human final decision-makers; not every possible AI workflow or a systematic evidence census

summary: Successful AI assistance requires both potential complementarity and effective human use of that potential. Source preferences depend on task, information and experience. More recent repeated-reliance studies summarized here do not support a universal algorithm-aversion claim; explanations can increase acceptance without improving correctness. Timing, confidence displays, cognitive limits and feedback must be assessed separately.

findings.definition: Giving greater weight or preference to algorithmic advice or judgment than to human advice or judgment in a comparable task.
findings.novelty_rationale: This is the comparative counterpart of algorithm aversion, not a synonym for uncritical automation bias. The preference can be justified by competence; automation bias additionally concerns inappropriate checking or reliance. The named concept appears in the review’s cited Logg title and its quantitative-task discussion.

evidence.quote: people actually prefer to take advice from algorithms

findings.evidence_scope: The read review summarizes algorithm-over-human advice preference in several low-stakes quantitative tasks and cites Logg, Minson and Moore 2019. The original Logg experiment was not independently read and is not added as if it were a second reviewed source.
findings.boundary: Appreciation is a relative source preference, not proof of excessive trust, moral endorsement, universal accuracy or a model’s personal liking. It may coexist with selective distrust on other items. Compare like-for-like task quality and expertise before labeling the preference a failure.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human source-preference findings summarized in a read narrative review; intrinsic AI preference mechanism untested
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI analogue: compare how an assistant weights matched advice labeled as algorithmic versus human while holding content, known performance and authority constant. Then vary actual reliability to distinguish source-label preference from appropriate use of better evidence.

findings.term: Repeated feedback can support selective reliance rather than blanket aversion
findings.definition: The review contrasts one-shot delegation after algorithm exposure with repeated tasks in which people can learn when their own or an AI’s advice is more reliable.
findings.novelty_rationale: A design- and experience-dependent qualification of the existing term, not a separate aversion type per experimental paradigm.
findings.evidence_scope: Narrative comparison of cited primary studies; some repeated-reliance work summarized here approaches optimal selective strategies, unlike a universal all-or-nothing aversion account.
findings.boundary: This is not evidence that all people eventually calibrate reliance or that all experience eliminates aversion. Repeated-task feedback, initial expectations, domain and outcome measure differ between studies.

findings.term: An explanation’s presence can become an unreliable reliance cue
findings.definition: Users may adopt advice more often when an explanation is present even if the explanation does not improve their ability to distinguish correct from incorrect advice.
findings.novelty_rationale: The pattern fits existing uncritical machine-advice reliance. No separate explanation-presence bias is created from the same outcome.

evidence.quote: appropriate levels of reliance and trust.

findings.evidence_scope: The review summarizes mixed feature-attribution findings and warns that convincingness and informative value are different objectives; it does not add a new randomized experiment itself.
findings.boundary: Increased acceptance, reported trust and objective accuracy are distinct. Neither all explanations nor all reliance are harmful, and source fluency or explanation length alone does not establish actual fidelity.

findings.term: More interface information can exceed human processing capacity
findings.definition: Additional model details or controls can impose cognitive demands that prevent a human decision-maker from using AI assistance effectively.
findings.novelty_rationale: Human information overload is an application of the existing cognitive-load entry, not a new label for the same limited-processing outcome.
findings.evidence_scope: Theoretical synthesis of cited interaction studies and cognitive-resource accounts; no single safe optimal explanation length or universal overload threshold is established.
findings.boundary: This evidence concerns human users. A model’s context-window errors and a user’s cognitive overload are different mechanisms; the former cannot be inferred from the latter. Simpler interfaces still need to preserve information necessary for informed oversight.

methodological_limits: The authors explicitly say this is not a systematic review; no exhaustive search, pooled effect estimate or universal consensus is inferred.
Much of the summarized evidence uses simple, low-stakes or wizard-of-Oz tasks; deployed model error correlations, expert performance and real consequences may differ.

A pair may lack statistical potential for complementarity because errors are correlated or abilities differ too greatly; failure to outperform both components does not by itself show a human reliance bias.
Statistical aggregation of independent human/AI predictions is not the same as a person making the final combined decision.
Accurate behavioral calibration need not prove a rich explicit theory of the AI; simple learned strategies may generate the same pattern.
Many studies cover one session or one decision, limiting claims about long-term autonomy, engagement and reliance.
Human preferences or beliefs about an AI’s mind and competence are not verified facts about actual model cognition.

cross_paper_learning.finding: This review cites Rastogi’s time-allocation work. Treat the citation as synthesis, not independent replication; the primary record preserves its subset benefits, aggregate null comparisons and conditional optimality assumptions.

Filiz explicitly uses a narrow known-superiority definition, while this review compares source preference and repeated selective reliance. These operational differences prevent a universal algorithm-aversion conclusion.
Interface engagement and subjective quality can improve without objective accuracy. The review’s warning about explanations supports retaining those outcome distinctions.

deferred.reason: The review describes advice discounting and cites relevant primary literature but does not independently test its egocentric mechanism; retain those studies as primary-source leads before a standalone entry.
An aggregate team-performance outcome may arise without any decision-maker error; do not automatically count it as an intrinsic new bias.

deferred.term: Concurrent, sequential, on-demand and time-delayed advice; adaptive nudging
deferred.reason: Interaction paradigms or interventions, not four new psychological behaviours. Their effectiveness depends on task, competence and feedback.

limitations: One new comparative preference concept is indexed with secondary-source evidence and an explicitly untested AI analogue.
The review is used to preserve counterevidence and task distinctions rather than to equate AI appreciation with an ethical violation.
